clue.text: Love act? No thanks

indicators.note: saying no to something refuses it, so the word for thanks is taken out of the longer word

parts.note: an act is a pretence put on for show
ta is British slang for thank you

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs off a romantic gesture: is love just a performance, no thanks?
explanation.walkthrough: Take TA out of AFFECTATION and AFFECTION is left; the question mark flags that 'act' must be read as a noun for pretence.
explanation.definitionFit: Fondness and tender warmth towards someone is a standard synonym for love.

clue.text: Head trip on drugs with a wicked white line?

indicators.note: someone on drugs is scrambled and disordered, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hallucinatory trip on drugs, complete with a line of white powder.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'white line' looks like cocaine, but it is the colour bar that apartheid drew between white South Africans and everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: South Africa's segregation regime was an evil policy separating races, a boundary drawn to keep white people apart.

clue.text: Ditch some gormless officers when heading north

indicators.note: in a down clue, heading north means reading the letters upwards, from bottom to top
only part of the following words is wanted, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: Getting rid of some incompetent officers as the troops march north.
explanation.definitionFit: A fosse is a defensive trench or moat around a fortification, so a ditch.

clue.text: Drug user director possibly put in the rear of shot

indicators.note: being put at the rear means coming after, so the director word follows the shot word

parts.note: to have a shot at something is to have a crack at it
a director, for example, heads an organisation

explanation.surface: A film director's character, a drug user, gets placed at the back of the shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' marks the director as one example of a head; 'shot' is an attempt, not a camera take.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone addicted to crack cocaine is a drug user; the word is slang for such an addict.

clue.text: Declaration of one leaning over worshipper

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the first part above the second

parts.note: what one says at a wedding: I do
a ship leaning to one side has a list

explanation.surface: Someone bends over and makes a declaration, as a worshipper might.
explanation.definitionFit: An idolist is one who worships idols, an idolater, so a kind of worshipper.

clue.text: Gossips with issues wanting successor of leader

indicators.note: wanting means needing in place of what is there, so the first letter gives way to a replacement

parts.note: issues and matters are both subjects to be dealt with
the leader of the word for issues is M, and the next letter of the alphabet is N

explanation.surface: People who gossip often have issues and want the leader replaced.
explanation.walkthrough: The leader is M, the first letter of MATTERS; its successor in the alphabet, N, takes its place.
explanation.definitionFit: To natter is to chat idly at length, so natters means gossips as a verb.

clue.text: One's to get in beer? Gangway!

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so these letters go inside the drink

parts.note: ale is a type of beer
one is I, plus the 's

explanation.surface: A pub shout: someone's trying to get a beer in, so make way!
explanation.definitionFit: A gangway is a passage between rows of seats, the same thing as an aisle.

clue.text: Excellent kind of meat served up in one helping?

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, with the 1 read as I

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: beef and lamb are red meat

explanation.surface: A waiter serves an excellent cut of meat, one helping on a plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Helping' looks like a portion of food, but here it means assisting.
explanation.definitionFit: An aider is a person who assists, so one helping in the sense of giving help.

clue.text: Tip to save a penny involving pliant plastic band

indicators.note: to involve is to take in, so the outer letters wrap around the rearranged ones
plastic can be moulded into a new shape, so these letters are rearranged
the tip of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
taken as written
p is the abbreviation for penny
taken as written, as fodder

explanation.surface: Money-saving advice involving a flexible plastic band.
explanation.walkthrough: The S and AP surround a shuffle of PLIANT. Spinal Tap is the fictional heavy-metal group in the mock documentary This Is Spinal Tap.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinal Tap is the spoof rock group from the 1984 film, so a musical band.

clue.text: Catholic caught in lie about brilliant success

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the word for lie runs backwards
something caught in another is held inside it

parts.note: a tale is a falsehood, as in telling tales
C is the abbreviation for Catholic

explanation.surface: A Catholic caught out in a lie, yet it turns into a triumph.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclat is borrowed from French for dazzling effect or conspicuous acclaim, a striking achievement.

clue.text: A boat user wrong to act stupidly

indicators.note: wrong means out of order, so the letters are put in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone using a boat badly is said to be fooling around.
explanation.walkthrough: To arse about is crude British slang for messing around.
explanation.definitionFit: The British slang phrase means to fool around or behave idiotically, wasting time.

clue.text: Vacuous dealer Hoskins will bore

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the inside of the word is removed and only its ends kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
the setter Hoskins says I'll, meaning I will

explanation.surface: An empty-headed card dealer complains the setter will be tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a tedious person, but it is the verb to make a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: To drill is to make a hole with a rotating tool, which is to bore.

clue.text: Golden Brown? Bit of wisdom in that tune

indicators.note: in that places the letter inside the colour word just given

parts.note: teak is a golden brown wood and colour

indicators.note: a bit of a word here is just its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Golden Brown, the Stranglers hit: is there a bit of wisdom in that song?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tune' looks like a song, but it is the verb meaning to adjust.
explanation.definitionFit: To tweak an engine or setting is to make fine adjustments to it, just as tuning does.

clue.text: A dizzying thing I catch around May?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: around places the catching word so it surrounds the name that follows

parts.note: to catch fish is to net them
Brian May is the guitarist of the rock band Queen

explanation.surface: Someone describes the giddy effect of catching sight of a pop star, or of a spring month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May' looks like the month, but it is the surname of Queen's guitarist, Brian May.
explanation.definitionFit: An inebriant is an intoxicant, a substance that makes you drunk and dizzy.

clue.text: Serious load of fuzz in the lughole?

indicators.note: one thing in another here means the second word comes first and the first follows

parts.note: lughole is British slang for the ear
a nest is a tangled mass, such as a clump of fluff

explanation.surface: A grave question about a great clump of fluff stuck in someone's ear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fuzz' might suggest police, but here it is fluff; read the answer as EAR NEST, a nest in the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnest means sincere and grave in intention, a straightforward synonym for serious.

clue.text: Event where one will see The Rolling Stones?

definitions.text: Event where one will see The Rolling Stones?

parts.words: Event where one will see The Rolling Stones?
parts.note: surface reading: a concert by the famous rock band
setter's reading: actual stones rolling down a slope

explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make it read as a Rolling Stones gig, but the stones are literal rocks tumbling downhill.
explanation.definitionFit: A mass of rock sliding down a hillside is exactly an event where stones are seen rolling.

clue.text: Street artist might do this over royal extension

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street
R stands for royal, as in RN or RAF
an artist may engrave a plate with acid

explanation.surface: A street artist at work painting over a royal portrait or image.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' places the artist's verb after the royal letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretch is an expanse or an added length, a lengthening, which is an extension.

clue.text: Excited kissers in a state of peril

indicators.note: excited means stirred up and agitated, so the letters are mixed around

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder

explanation.surface: Passionate kissers caught somewhere dangerous.
explanation.definitionFit: Riskiness is the quality of being hazardous or dangerous, a condition of peril.

clue.text: Reckless as someone diving into The Sun?

definitions.note: a cryptic description; the answer describes such a person rather than naming them
definitions.meaning: second meaning, taken literally: whoever plunged into a star would have a scorching head

explanation.walkthrough: The capitals suggest the tabloid newspaper, but the joke is a literal dive into the star, which would leave you with a hot head.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot-headed person acts rashly without thinking, impetuous and quick-tempered, so reckless.

clue.text: Crucial match papers covered in December outside of Exeter

indicators.note: something covered in another is wrapped inside it

parts.note: Dec is the calendar abbreviation

indicators.note: the outside of a word is its first and last letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the city
identity papers are ID

explanation.surface: Newspapers in Exeter cover a big December fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' looks like newspapers, but it means identity documents.
explanation.definitionFit: A decider is the final game that settles a tied contest, so it is the match that matters most.

clue.text: Rosy's fed up with a bit of iceberg Ed prepared

indicators.note: being fed with something means having it put inside

parts.note: rosy means pinkish red
taken as written

indicators.note: a bit of a word here is just its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Rosy is fed up with Ed, who got a lettuce ready for the salad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fed up' reads as annoyed, but it means RED is filled with A. Iceberg is a type of lettuce.
explanation.definitionFit: To ready something is to make it prepared, so readied is the past tense meaning prepared.

clue.text: Old drunk drunks facing off around back of Co-op

indicators.note: two figures facing off stand nose to nose, so the first is turned around to face the second
around places the pair so they surround the letter taken from the shop

parts.note: two sots, a sot being a drunkard

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of the shop's name

explanation.surface: Two old drunks squaring up to each other round the back of the Co-op supermarket.
explanation.walkthrough: Two sots face each other, the first reversed, giving TOS SOT; P goes inside. The Co-op is a British chain of shops.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosspot is an old-fashioned word for a habitual drinker, someone who tosses back pots of ale.

clue.text: Barrel full of rare drink arrives

indicators.note: a vessel full of something holds it inside

parts.note: a tun is a large cask
R is an abbreviation for rare
to sup is to sip a drink

explanation.surface: A cask full of some rare beverage is delivered.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn up is to appear or show up at a place, the phrasal verb for arriving.

clue.text: Buggy PC with harsh UI in need of fixing

indicators.note: something in need of fixing is broken, so these letters are rearranged into working order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A personal computer with a buggy, unfriendly user interface that needs repair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buggy' looks like the computer-glitch adjective, but it is the noun for a baby's carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A pushchair, the British term for a stroller, is also called a baby buggy.

clue.text: Dispatches head of state kept in pockets

indicators.note: something kept in another is held within it

parts.note: in snooker, to pocket a ball is to pot it

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Government dispatches, with the head of state pocketing something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dispatches' looks like a noun for reports, but it is the verb for sending by mail.
explanation.definitionFit: To post a letter is to send it off by mail, so posts means dispatches.

clue.text: In which millions will be stolen from van?

definitions.text: In which millions will be stolen from van?

indicators.note: what is stolen from something is taken away, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a camper van, or simply a camper
M is the abbreviation for millions

explanation.surface: A heist movie: a gang steal millions from a security van.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a heist in which millions are stolen from a van is just such a caper.
explanation.definitionFit: Caper is slang for a crime, especially a daring robbery, the kind of heist where a cash van gets raided.

clue.text: After removing top, circulate fire in Fife

indicators.note: the top of an across word is its first letter, which is taken away

parts.note: at a party you circulate, or mingle, among the guests

explanation.surface: Instructions for spreading a fire across the Scottish county of Fife once the lid is off.
explanation.walkthrough: Fife is a county in Scotland; 'in Fife' marks the answer as a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingle is a Scottish word for a fire burning on a hearth, as in inglenook.

clue.text: Cotton on jacket from George starts to tear in trolley

indicators.note: a jacket is an outer layer, so only the outside letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the name

indicators.note: the starts of words are their first letters

parts.note: the opening letters of each of these words

explanation.surface: A cotton jacket from the supermarket clothing range George rips in the shopping trolley.
explanation.walkthrough: George is the clothing brand sold at Asda, a British supermarket; 'Cotton on' is the definition, not the fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: To cotton on is to grasp or understand something, which is what you do when you finally get it.

clue.text: Miss out to save money might do this?

definitions.text: Miss out to save money might do this?

indicators.note: to save something is to keep it safe within, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: to skip something is to miss it out
M is the abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: Someone trying to save money might go without things.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines the answer: missing out on things to save money is exactly how you skimp.
explanation.definitionFit: To skimp is to economise by spending too little, cutting corners to keep costs down.

clue.text: Vetted various pints with editor around city

indicators.note: around places the earlier letters so they surround the city
various means assorted, so the letters come in a mixed order

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder
ed is short for editor
EC is the postcode of the City of London

explanation.surface: An editor checks out different pints around town.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, whose postcode begins EC.
explanation.definitionFit: To vet something is to check it carefully, so vetted and inspected are both past tenses of examining.

clue.text: Promise to use bad language

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to vow or pledge

explanation.surface: Someone vowing to curse.
explanation.definitionFit: One verb covers both taking an oath, as in court, and cursing with profanities.

clue.text: Ousted from office (after having sex inside laid down)

indicators.note: to have something inside is to hold it within, so the short word goes in the middle

parts.note: a deposed ruler has been removed from power
it is a euphemism for sex

explanation.surface: A politician thrown out of office after a sex scandal, then laid low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid down' could suggest a bed, but it is the definition: deposited as in placed.
explanation.definitionFit: To deposit something is to set it down or put it in place, as sediment is laid down.
